findings.blocking_reason: Adding an unimplemented @abc.abstractmethod to StatefulDetectorHandler makes the only concrete subclass, MetricAlertDetectorHandler, uninstantiable, causing a pipeline-wide regression for all metric-alert detectors.
findings.body: The PR adds `build_occurrence_and_event_data` as an `@abc.abstractmethod` on `StatefulDetectorHandler` (detector.py:166-170) and calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(...)` on every non-OK status transition (detector.py:299-301). `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` in `src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py:11` is the ONLY concrete `StatefulDetectorHandler` subclass in the codebase, and its body is just `pass` — it does not implement the new abstract method. As a result, `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` can no longer be instantiated: any access to `detector.detector_handler` for a `metric_alert_fire` detector executes `group_type.detector_handler(self)` (workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86), which raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods build_occurrence_and_event_data`. This is a pipeline-wide regression: every metric-alert detector fails at handler construction, before any evaluation, state transition, or Kafka emission occurs. The downstream consumer safety checks (allow_ingest / per-fingerprint rate limiting) and the INGEST_OCCURRENCES volume caveats are therefore moot for metric-alert detectors — no occurrence is ever produced because the handler cannot be built. The individual findings (behavior change, consumer safety, volume caveat, missing implementation) each describe a narrow concern; together they obscure that the only registered stateful detector handler is now uninstantiable, which breaks the whole metric-alert flow rather than just the newly-added non-OK emission branch.
findings.evidence: detector.py:166-170 declares `@abc.abstractmethod def build_occurrence_and_event_data(self, group_key, value, new_status) -> tuple[IssueOccurrence, dict[str, Any]]: pass` on `StatefulDetectorHandler`. detector.py:298-301 calls it on every non-OK transition: `else: result, event_data = self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))`. src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py:11-12: `class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass` — the only concrete StatefulDetectorHandler subclass in the repo (grep for `StatefulDetectorHandler` shows only this subclass). src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86: `return group_type.detector_handler(self)` — instantiates the handler class; this raises TypeError for MetricAlertDetectorHandler because the abstract method is unimplemented. src/sentry/issues/grouptype.py:161 + incidents/grouptype.py:27 wire `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, so every `metric_alert_fire` detector is affected.
findings.suggestion: Either (a) implement `build_occurrence_and_event_data` on `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` (build a real IssueOccurrence for metric-alert fires), or (b) provide a default implementation on `StatefulDetectorHandler` that raises a clear NotImplementedError / returns a no-op for detectors that don't yet support occurrence emission (preserving the previous `result = None` behavior), or (c) gate the non-OK emission branch on a capability check (e.g. `hasattr(self, 'build_occurrence_and_event_data')` or a handler flag) so handlers that haven't opted in keep the old StatusChangeMessage/None behavior. At minimum, add a unit test that instantiates every registered `detector_handler` class to catch abstract-method regressions before they reach production.
findings.title: New abstract method build_occurrence_and_event_data makes MetricAlertDetectorHandler non-instantiable, breaking the entire metric-alert detector pipeline (not just the new non-OK emission path)

findings.blocking_reason: Adding a new abstract method to the base class without implementing it in the only production subclass makes MetricAlertDetectorHandler uninstantiable, a regression that breaks existing behavior at runtime.
findings.body: A new abstract method `build_occurrence_and_event_data(self, group_key, value, new_status: PriorityLevel) -> tuple[IssueOccurrence, dict[str, Any]]` was added to `StatefulDetectorHandler` in `src/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/detector.py` (lines 166-170, decorated with `@abc.abstractmethod`). The only concrete `StatefulDetectorHandler` subclass in the production codebase, `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` in `src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py` (lines 11-12), consists solely of `class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass` and does NOT override `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Because the new method is `@abc.abstractmethod`, any attempt to instantiate `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract method build_occurrence_and_event_data`. This class is wired as `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` (grouptype.py line 27), so constructing that detector handler is now impossible. The downstream consequence is exactly what the obligation warns about: no occurrence can be produced, so issue grouping/dedup (which relies on `build_fingerprint` feeding a stable-fingerprint `IssueOccurrence` returned from `build_occurrence_and_event_data`) cannot run for metric alerts. The base `evaluate_group_key_value` calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))` at detector.py line 299 whenever `new_status != DetectorPriorityLevel.OK`, so any non-resolve state transition hits the unimplemented method. The test handler `MockDetectorStateHandler` in `tests/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/test_detector.py` line 36 does implement it, confirming the method is required for instantiation and that the production subclass was not updated to match. The two ends disagree: the base class requires the method, the concrete subclass does not provide it.
findings.suggestion: Either (a) implement `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (and the remaining abstractmethods `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`) on `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` so it produces an `IssueOccurrence` with a fingerprint derived from `self.build_fingerprint(group_key)` for stable dedup, plus the `event_data` dict the kafka consumer expects; or (b) if `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` is intentionally still a stub (the file's TODO `"This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction"` suggests so), mark it abstract as well and stop wiring it as `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` until it is implemented, so the abstract-method contract is not violated at instantiation time.
findings.title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler does not implement abstract build_occurrence_and_event_data, blocking instantiation

findings.blocking_reason: This is a test-fidelity and coverage issue (mock helper ignores a parameter, wrong expected value in a test) — production code passes the correct value; no build, security, data, API, or behavioral regression is demonstrated.
findings.body:
This PR introduces `build_occurrence_and_event_data` as a subclass-overridable hook on `StatefulDetectorHandler` (production call at detector.py:299-300: `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))`). The hook's `value` argument carries the actual group value from the data packet through `evaluate_group_key_value` into occurrence construction — a brand new abstraction boundary that did not exist in the old inline construction.

The entire test suite for the stateful detector pipeline exercises this hook through exactly ONE implementation: `MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data` (line 36-39) delegates to `build_mock_occurrence_and_event`. That helper (line 244-275) binds `value` in its signature but never references it — `evidence_data={}` is empty, no field on `IssueOccurrence` or `event_data` encodes `value`. So the mock makes `value` a decorative parameter.

Compounding this, the only multi-group test (`test_state_results_multi_group`, line 175-205) builds its expected `group_2` occurrence with `value=6` (line 191) when production would pass `value=10` (data packet line 177: `group_vals={"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}`). The test passes today only because the helper ignores `value`.

Together these create a complete test-contract vacuum for the new hook:

1. No test verifies that `value` flows from `evaluate_group_key_value` (detector.py:299-300) into the subclass hook. A future subclass could silently drop `value`, swap it with `group_key`, or hardcode it — and produce an identical mock occurrence, so every test would still pass.

2. The wrong-value (6) is actively codified in the test's expected occurrence. If someone "fixes" the helper to embed `value` (e.g. in `evidence_data`), `test_state_results_multi_group` will assert that `6` flows through for `group_2`, when production actually passes `10`. The fix would surface as a test failure that encodes the WRONG expectation — a masking inversion that could mislead a developer into "correcting" production to pass 6, or into weakening the assertion instead of fixing the test data.

3. This is a regression-risk asymmetry introduced by the PR: the old inline construction in `evaluate_group_key_value` had no abstraction boundary where `value` could be lost. The new hook creates that boundary, and the test suite provides zero enforcement that the boundary preserves `value`. The two findings are not independent test smells — they are a shared mechanism: the decorative parameter is precisely what hides the wrong-value assertion, and the wrong-value assertion is precisely what would mask a real value-propagation regression if the helper were ever fixed.

An individual reviewer seeing finding A ("helper ignores value") might conclude it's a minor test-fidelity nit. An individual reviewer seeing finding B ("wrong value 6 vs 10") might conclude the same. The compound view shows the test suite has no oracle for the hook's `value` contract at all — the hook is a new public surface with no enforcement, and the one test that should catch value-propagation regressions actively encodes the wrong expectation.
findings.evidence:
Step 1 (hook is new and public): detector.py:299-300 calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))` where `value` is the real group value from the packet. This is a subclass-overridable method on StatefulDetectorHandler.

Step 2 (only one mock implementation): MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data (test_detector.py:36-39) is the sole test implementation, delegating to build_mock_occurrence_and_event.

Step 3 (helper ignores value): build_mock_occurrence_and_event (test_detector.py:244-275) binds `value: int` but never references it. IssueOccurrence (lines 251-266) uses `evidence_data={}` and event_data (lines 267-274) has no value field. Occurrences are identical for value=6, value=10, or any int.

Step 4 (test codifies wrong value): test_state_results_multi_group (line 177) builds data_packet with group_vals={"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}. Line 191 builds expected occurrence_2 with value=6 instead of 10. Test passes because of Step 3.

Step 5 (compound escalation): If the helper is fixed to use `value` (e.g. evidence_data={"value": value}), line 191's expected occurrence would encode value=6, but production passes 10 → test fails with the WRONG expectation encoded, risking a misleading "fix". If the helper is NOT fixed, any real value-propagation regression (drop, swap, hardcode) is invisible. Either branch of the decision tree leaves the hook's value contract unenforced.

Step 6 (regression asymmetry): Pre-PR, evaluate_group_key_value constructed occurrences inline — no abstraction boundary where value could be lost. Post-PR, the hook creates that boundary. The test suite provides zero enforcement at the new boundary, and the one multi-group test encodes the wrong expected value. Net effect: the PR widens the test-coverage surface without adding any oracle for the newly exposed contract.
findings.suggestion:
Make `value` a verifiable part of the mock occurrence AND correct the test data, in one change, so the test suite becomes a real oracle for the hook's value contract:

1. In `build_mock_occurrence_and_event`, embed `value` in a field that survives comparison, e.g. `evidence_data={"value": value}` on the `IssueOccurrence` (line 259), and add `"value": value` to `event_data` (lines 267-274).

2. In `test_state_results_multi_group` line 191, change the `value` argument from `6` to `10` to match the data packet at line 177.

3. Audit the other tests that call `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` (test_state_results, test_results_on_change, test_dedupe, TestEvaluate.test) and confirm each passes the value that production would pass for that group, so the assertions genuinely verify the value-propagation chain `data_packet.group_vals → evaluate_group_key_value → build_occurrence_and_event_data → IssueOccurrence.evidence_data`.

This converts the helper from a decorative parameter into a value-propagation oracle and closes the test-contract vacuum at the new hook boundary.
findings.title: New build_occurrence_and_event_data hook has zero test enforcement of its value contract: the only mock implementation ignores value AND the only multi-group test codifies the wrong expected value (6 vs 10)

findings.blocking_reason: The finding itself confirms this is not reachable in production today—process_detectors has zero production callers and the module is clearly WIP scaffolding.
findings.body:
StatefulDetectorHandler declares four @abstractmethod methods that this class does not implement: counter_names (property) at detector.py:142-148, get_dedupe_value at detector.py:150-156, get_group_key_values at detector.py:158-164, build_occurrence_and_event_data at detector.py:166-170 (NEW in this PR). DetectorHandler.evaluate (line 125-129) is also abstract, but StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate (line 226-244) provides a concrete implementation, so that one is satisfied via inheritance.

Impact: Any code path that calls detector.detector_handler (→ group_type.detector_handler(self) at models/detector.py:86) for a Detector row whose type == "metric_alert_fire" will raise TypeError: Cannot instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract method(s) counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data.

Reachability today: Not live. process_detectors (processors/detector.py:47) is the only production caller of .detector_handler, and it has zero production callers — only 5 references in tests/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/test_detector.py. The workflow_engine module shows multiple WIP signals (hardcoded project_id=1 at models/detector.py:54-56, TODO on grouptype.py:10, "We don't create these issues yet" on MetricAlertFire). So this is a latent landmine, not a live break.

Why this matters anyway: The handler is registered on MetricAlertFire.detector_handler (line 27), so the contract is "this group type has a working detector handler." The moment process_detectors (or any new caller) is wired into production for metric alerts, this explodes. The PR repoints from DetectorHandler (where a stub evaluate returning [] was the only unimplemented piece) to StatefulDetectorHandler (where four concrete implementations are now required) — so the PR widens the gap rather than closing it.

The test subclass MockDetectorStateHandler (in tests/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/test_detector.py) implements all four — confirming the contract is satisfiable and that MetricAlertDetectorHandler is the outlier, not StatefulDetectorHandler.

No other issues found: The repoint from DetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate] to StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate] is otherwise type-correct — the generic parameter matches, and StatefulDetectorHandler is a proper subclass of DetectorHandler. No other production StatefulDetectorHandler subclasses exist to break against the newly-added build_occurrence_and_event_data abstractmethod (only MetricAlertDetectorHandler in src and MockDetectorStateHandler in tests). The evaluate return-type change on DetectorHandler ([] → dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]) is consistent with StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate's concrete implementation at line 226-244, which builds exactly that dict shape.
findings.suggestion:
1. If this PR is intentionally WIP scaffolding (consistent with the TODO on line 10 and the placeholder pass body): add a clear comment on the class documenting that it's a non-functional placeholder and that instantiation will fail, so the next contributor doesn't assume the registration implies a working handler. Consider gating the registration behind a feature flag or leaving detector_handler = None until the implementations land.
2. If this PR is meant to be functional: implement all four abstractmethods before merging. build_occurrence_and_event_data is the one newly added this PR, but the other three were already required by StatefulDetectorHandler and remain unimplemented.
findings.title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is non-instantiable (latent TypeError)

findings.blocking_reason: The finding explicitly confirms this TypeError is pre-existing — the class was already non-instantiable before this PR due to the same missing abstractmethod, so the PR does not introduce a regression.
findings.body:
The live production call site `Detector.detector_handler` (line 86) executes `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, which instantiates the handler class registered on the `GroupType`. For any `Detector` row with `type == "metric_alert_fire"`, `self.group_type` returns `MetricAlertFire` (auto-registered via `GroupType.__init_subclass__` at `src/sentry/issues/grouptype.py:163-165`), and `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler` is `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` (`src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py:27`).

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` is declared as `class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass` (`src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py:11-12`) — a `pass`-only body that implements **none** of the 5 abstractmethods now required by `StatefulDetectorHandler` (`evaluate`, `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). Attempting `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(self)` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`.

**Important context on pre-existing status**: This break is NOT newly introduced by this PR's diff to `detector.py`. Before the PR, `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` subclassed `DetectorHandler` (which has `@abc.abstractmethod evaluate`) with the same `pass` body, so it was **already non-instantiable** — the call at line 86 would have raised `TypeError` for the same reason (missing `evaluate`). The PR's repointing to `StatefulDetectorHandler` (in `grouptype.py`, not this file) expands the set of unimplemented abstractmethods from 1 to 5, but the instantiation failure is identical.

**Why this matters for this PR**: The diff to `detector.py` itself is a clean, behavior-preserving refactor (extracting `group_type` into a reusable property at lines 58-60). No new bug is introduced in this file. However, the PR's companion change in `grouptype.py` deliberately moves the placeholder class to a new base without implementing the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` hook, so the handler remains non-instantiable. The TODO on `grouptype.py:10` ("This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction") flags this as intentionally incomplete, but the class is still registered as `detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler` on `MetricAlertFire`, meaning any `metric_alert_fire` detector entering `process_detectors` will crash at line 86.

**Reachability**: `process_detectors` (`src/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/detector.py:47-70`) iterates detectors and calls `handler = detector.detector_handler` at line 53. If a `Detector` with `type="metric_alert_fire"` exists in the database and is passed to `process_detectors`, the TypeError fires. There is no upstream guard that filters out `metric_alert_fire` detectors before this point.
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `process_detectors(data_packet, detectors)` at `src/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/detector.py:47` iterates `detectors`.
Step 2: Line 53 calls `handler = detector.detector_handler` for each detector.
Step 3: `Detector.detector_handler` property at `src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:63` calls `self.group_type` (line 64), which returns `grouptype.registry.get_by_slug(self.type)` (line 60).
Step 4: For `self.type == "metric_alert_fire"`, `registry.get_by_slug` returns `MetricAlertFire` (registered via `__init_subclass__` → `registry.add(cls)` at `src/sentry/issues/grouptype.py:163-165`; `MetricAlertFire.slug = "metric_alert_fire"` at `src/sentry/incidents/grouptype.py:20`).
Step 5: Line 76 checks `group_type.detector_handler` — `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler` (grouptype.py:27), which is truthy, so the guard passes.
Step 6: Line 86 executes `return group_type.detector_handler(self)` → `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(self)`.
Step 7: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` is `class MetricAlertDetectorHandler(StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]): pass` (grouptype.py:11-12) — does not implement `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (new abstractmethod at `processors/detector.py:166-170`), nor `evaluate`, `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`.
Step 8: Python raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods build_occurrence_and_event_data, counter_names, evaluate, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values`.
findings.suggestion: Since this is a known placeholder (TODO on grouptype.py:10), two options: (1) Implement `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (and the other 4 abstractmethods) on `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now, if the metric alert flow is meant to be live. (2) If the handler is intentionally not yet built, add a defensive guard in `Detector.detector_handler` (or in `process_detectors`) to skip handlers that cannot be instantiated — e.g., catch `TypeError` at line 86 and log a warning + return `None`, similar to the existing `if not group_type.detector_handler` guard at line 76. This prevents a hard crash for any `metric_alert_fire` detector that reaches this path. Option (2) is the minimal change; option (1) is the complete fix.
findings.title: Confirmed TypeError blast radius for metric_alert_fire detectors via detector_handler property — pre-existing break expanded by PR's repointing to StatefulDetectorHandler

findings.blocking_reason: This is a latent test helper quality issue where the test passes despite a wrong mock value; it does not break the build, production behavior, or any existing contract.
findings.body:
In `test_state_results_multi_group`, the data packet at line 177 is constructed with `{"dedupe": 2, "group_vals": {"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}}`. Production code at `detector.py:299-300` calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))` where `value` is the actual group value from the packet (so `10` for `group_2`). However, the test's expected occurrence for `group_2` is built at line 190-191 with `value=6`:

```python
occurrence_2, event_data_2 = build_mock_occurrence_and_event(
    detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH
)
```

This should be `10` to faithfully mirror what production would pass. The test currently passes only because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores its `value` parameter entirely (see related finding). If the mock helper is ever fixed to use `value` (e.g. embedding it in `evidence_data`), this test will fail or — worse — silently assert against the wrong value, masking real value-propagation regressions in `evaluate_group_key_value`.
findings.evidence: Step 1: test_state_results_multi_group builds DataPacket at line 177 with group_vals={"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}. Step 2: process_detectors calls handler.evaluate(data_packet) (detector.py:58). Step 3: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate iterates group_values.items() (detector.py:238) and calls evaluate_group_key_value(group_key='group_2', value=10, ...). Step 4: evaluate_group_key_value at detector.py:299-300 calls self.build_occurrence_and_event_data('group_2', 10, PriorityLevel.HIGH). Step 5: But the test's expected occurrence_2 at line 191 is built with value=6, not 10. Step 6: The test passes only because build_mock_occurrence_and_event (line 244-275) never references its `value` parameter, so 6 and 10 produce identical occurrences. The mismatch is latent.
findings.suggestion: Change the `value` argument on line 191 from `6` to `10` to match the data packet. Better yet, make `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` actually use `value` (e.g. in `evidence_data` or an assertion field) so the test genuinely verifies that the value flows from the data packet through `evaluate_group_key_value` into `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.
findings.title: test_state_results_multi_group builds group_2 expected occurrence with wrong value (6 vs 10)

findings.blocking_reason: This is a test coverage gap (missing verification of value propagation in a mock helper), not a production bug, build break, or behavior regression.
findings.body:
The extracted helper `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` declares `value: int` in its signature (line 246-247) but the function body (lines 250-274) never references `value`. The produced `IssueOccurrence` and `event_data` are identical regardless of whether `value` is 6, 10, or any other integer. This is the only mock implementation of `build_occurrence_and_event_data` in the test suite (wired in via `MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data` at line 36-39), so the entire test suite for the stateful detector pipeline has zero coverage that the `value` argument is correctly propagated from `evaluate_group_key_value` (detector.py:300) into the subclass hook.

This is a regression risk introduced by this PR: the old inline construction in `evaluate_group_key_value` didn't have a hook, so there was no abstraction boundary where `value` could be lost. Now that `build_occurrence_and_event_data` is a subclass-overridable hook, a future implementation could silently drop or miswire `value`, and no test would catch it.
findings.evidence: Step 1: MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data (line 36-39) delegates to build_mock_occurrence_and_event(self, group_key, value, new_status). Step 2: build_mock_occurrence_and_event (line 244-275) binds `value` but never uses it in the IssueOccurrence constructor (lines 251-266) or event_data dict (lines 267-274). Step 3: Production evaluate_group_key_value at detector.py:299-300 calls self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status)) where value is the real group value. Step 4: Any bug where `value` is mis-passed (e.g. swapped with group_key, or hardcoded) would produce an identical mock occurrence, so the test would still pass. Step 5: Confirmed by the group_2 mismatch in test_state_results_multi_group (line 191 passes 6 instead of 10) — the test passes despite the wrong value.
findings.suggestion: Incorporate `value` into the mock occurrence in a verifiable way — e.g. add `"value": value` to `event_data`, or set `evidence_data={"value": value}` on the `IssueOccurrence`. Then update assertions in test_state_results, test_state_results_multi_group, test_results_on_change, test_dedupe, and test (TestEvaluate) to assert the correct value flows through. This converts the helper from a decorative parameter into a real value-propagation oracle.

findings.body:

This means the `TypeError` blast radius described in the companion finding is not caught by CI — the test suite passes despite a live production path being broken.

This is a pre-existing coverage gap (not introduced by this PR's refactor of `detector.py`), but the PR's repointing of `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` to `StatefulDetectorHandler` (in `grouptype.py`) makes the gap more consequential because the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` abstractmethod is the hook that the PR is built around — if a future PR implements the handler without realizing the test gap, regressions could go undetected.
findings.evidence:
Step 1: Searched `tests/sentry/workflow_engine/` for `metric_alert_fire|MetricAlertFire|MetricAlertDetectorHandler` → 0 matches.
Step 2: The only handler classes exercised in `tests/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/test_detector.py` are `MockDetectorHandler` (line 69) and `MockDetectorStateHandler` (line 76), both of which implement the required abstractmethods.

findings.suggestion: Add a test that constructs a `Detector` with `type="metric_alert_fire"` and asserts that `detector.detector_handler` raises `TypeError` (documenting the known placeholder state), OR add a test that verifies the defensive guard recommended in the companion finding (graceful skip instead of crash). findings.blocking_reason: The finding explicitly confirms this is not a live bug; the conversion is currently safe and this is a defensive-coding/contract-clarity suggestion.
findings.body:
The conversion `PriorityLevel(new_status)` at line 300 is **currently safe** because it sits in the `else` branch of `if new_status == DetectorPriorityLevel.OK` (line 290), so `new_status` is guaranteed to be `LOW`, `MEDIUM`, or `HIGH` at that point — all of which have valid `PriorityLevel` counterparts (values 25/50/75). `DetectorPriorityLevel.OK` (value 0) has no `PriorityLevel` equivalent, so `PriorityLevel(DetectorPriorityLevel.OK)` would raise `ValueError: 0 is not a valid PriorityLevel`.

However, the safety of this conversion depends entirely on the structural adjacency of the `if/else` branches. The invariant "new_status != OK at line 300" is not enforced at the conversion site itself — it is an emergent property of the surrounding control flow. This is fragile for two reasons:

1. **Refactoring risk.** If a future change restructures the status check (e.g. flattens the if/else, adds an early-return path, or moves the occurrence construction into a helper), the conversion can silently end up reachable with `new_status == OK`, producing a runtime `ValueError` that is not caught anywhere. There is no assertion, comment, or type-level constraint at line 300 that signals "this conversion is only valid for non-OK statuses."

2. **Hook contract ambiguity.** `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (line 166-170) is a **public method** (no underscore prefix) declared `@abc.abstractmethod` on `StatefulDetectorHandler`. Its signature accepts `new_status: PriorityLevel`, which already excludes OK by type construction. But the method is callable directly by subclasses or any code holding a `StatefulDetectorHandler` reference. A subclass that calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(gk, val, PriorityLevel(some_detector_status))` with `some_detector_status == DetectorPriorityLevel.OK` would hit the same `ValueError` before the hook body even runs. The hook's type contract (`PriorityLevel`, not `DetectorPriorityLevel`) hides the fact that the caller must perform the OK-filtering *before* the conversion, not after.

**Reachability of the live bug:** I verified there is exactly one call site of `build_occurrence_and_event_data` in the codebase — line 300 in `evaluate_group_key_value` (confirmed via grep: only `detector.py` and the test file reference the method). The `else` branch correctly guards it today, so this is **not a live bug**. It is a defensive-coding/contract-clarity concern.

**Semantic note:** `PriorityLevel` intentionally has no `OK` equivalent — `OK` means "no issue", so there is no priority to assign. This is a meaningful semantic distinction that should be documented at the conversion site, since the type system cannot enforce it (both enums are `IntEnum` and `DetectorPriorityLevel` is a superset of `PriorityLevel`'s values).
findings.evidence:
Step 1: `evaluate_group_key_value` (detector.py:246) computes `new_status: DetectorPriorityLevel` via `max()` over condition evaluations (line 280), starting from `DetectorPriorityLevel.OK` (line 271).
Step 2: Line 285 checks `if state_data.status != new_status:`; inside, line 290 checks `if new_status == DetectorPriorityLevel.OK:` → builds `StatusChangeMessage`.
Step 3: The `else` branch (line 298-301) calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status))`.
Step 4: `PriorityLevel` (src/sentry/types/group.py:63-66) defines only `LOW=25, MEDIUM=50, HIGH=75`. `DetectorPriorityLevel.OK=0` (src/sentry/workflow_engine/types.py:9) has no matching member.
Step 5: `PriorityLevel(0)` raises `ValueError: 0 is not a valid PriorityLevel`. This path is currently unreachable because the `else` branch only runs when `new_status != OK`, but no assertion or comment at line 300 documents this invariant.
Step 6: Grep confirms `build_occurrence_and_event_data` has exactly one production call site (detector.py:300). No other caller passes OK today.
findings.suggestion:
Pick one of the following (in order of preference):

1. **Assert the invariant at the conversion site** — makes the contract explicit and fails loudly on refactor:
```python
else:
    assert new_status != DetectorPriorityLevel.OK, "OK status must be handled by the StatusChangeMessage branch"
    result, event_data = self.build_occurrence_and_event_data(
        group_key, value, PriorityLevel(new_status)
    )
```

2. **Add a documenting comment** at line 300 explaining why the conversion is safe and that `PriorityLevel` intentionally excludes OK ("OK means 'no issue', so no priority").

3. **Map defensively** if there's any chance future code could reach this path with OK — e.g. fall back to `PriorityLevel.LOW` or skip occurrence emission, though this changes semantics and is less preferred than making the invariant explicit.

Option 1 is cheapest and most robust. The assertion documents the invariant and turns a silent future regression into a loud test failure.
findings.title: PriorityLevel(new_status) conversion relies on an implicit invariant; a defensive guard or documented contract would be more robust

findings.blocking_reason: Stale docstring is a documentation issue that does not break the build, tests, or runtime behavior.
findings.body:
The docstring on `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` (lines 229-233) was not updated when the return type changed from `list[DetectorEvaluationResult]` to `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. It still reads:

```python
"""
Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`.
There will be one result for each group key result in the packet, unless the
evaluation is skipped due to various rules.
"""
```

The signature on line 228 correctly declares `-> dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but the prose says 'list'. The second sentence about 'one result for each group key' is also now slightly misleading since the dict keys are group keys and duplicate group keys collapse via last-write-wins (line 243). Maintainers reading the docstring will be misled about the container type and the dedup semantics.
findings.evidence: Step 1: detector.py:228 signature is `def evaluate(self, data_packet: DataPacket[T]) -> dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]:`. Step 2: detector.py:230 docstring says 'returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`'. Step 3: The return statement at line 244 returns `results` which is a dict built via `results[result.group_key] = result` (line 243). Step 4: The docstring contradicts the signature and the implementation.
findings.suggestion: Update the docstring to: 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a dict of `DetectorEvaluationResult` keyed by `DetectorGroupKey`. There will be at most one result per group key (last-write-wins); evaluations are skipped per the dedupe and condition-group rules below.'
findings.title: Stale docstring: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate says 'returns a list' but now returns a dict

This is a pre-existing issue (present before the PR's refactor — the original code had the same `str(group_type)` in the same branch). The PR's extraction of `group_type` into a property didn't change this behavior. Flagging only as a nitpick since it doesn't affect functionality.

Step 1: `detector_handler` property at line 63 calls `self.group_type` (line 64), which returns `grouptype.registry.get_by_slug(self.type)` — returns `None` if slug not found.
